newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonia reaps reward of reform with EU invite.
newsitem.headline: Estonia reaps reward of reform with EU invite.

text.p: The tiny Baltic state of Estonia reaped the reward of its rush to ditch 50 years of Soviet rule with the European Commission's decision on Thursday that it should be among the first wave of EU entrants, analysts said.
The nation of just 1.5 million people has marked itself out as a radical economic reformer since quitting the former Soviet Union in 1991, earning itself the nickname "Baltic Tiger".
Its reward came as the Commission in Brussels agreed in principle to recommend talks with Estonia, Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary in the EU's first eastern enlargement.
"It can be said that they have been one of the best reformers," said International Monetary Fund (IMF) Estonia and Latvia representative Dimitri Demekas.

"Despite the fact there are now certain question marks about their macroeconomic perfomance, with the appropriate measures they have the chance to continue being in the forefront of reform," Demekas added.
Despite a growing trade deficit, Estonia saw growth of four percent in 1996. Its inflation is now at 10.8 percent, a stark contrast to the hyper-inflation of the post-Soviet era.

"We are happy that the European Commission has agreed to recommend Estonia to begin talks in the first wave and that they appreciate the economic reforms that Estonia has undertaken," said foreign ministry spokeswoman Ehtel Halliste.
Estonia and Baltic neighbours Latvia and Lithuania have all distinguished themselves from other former Soviet states as Western-oriented, determined reformers.
But Estonia began its economic transformation earlier, helped by a first post-independence government of radical free-marketeers.
Many Western companies also say Estonia is more business-friendly, with a strong practical streak which means legislation makes life easier rather than harder.

The desperate rush to leave the Communist era behind it means the capital Tallinn is a bustling, commercial centre with gleaming bank buildings springing up as it strives to become a modern Western-style capital city.
But the path to the EU will be still be tough for Estonia as its relations with huge neighbour Russia are tense and fractious.
Russia objects to the fact that the hundreds of thousands of Russian-speakers living in Estonia were not granted automatic citizenship after the country regained its independence.
Diplomats say relations will have to be improved before Estonia can finally enter the trading bloc.
